{"id": "80:6/q06", "question": "How is taṣaddā read and formed?", "turns_on": "Whether the original two tāʾs are reduced by deletion or assimilation, retained, or the verb is read with a prefixed ḍamma; transmitters' attributions differ.", "positions": [{"id": "80:6/q06/p1", "position": "A light ṣād in taṣaddā results from dropping one of the two tāʾs of tataṣaddā.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Naḥḥās, al-Fārisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Qurṭubī, and others explain deletion as easing the meeting of two tāʾs. Attributions include Kūfans and Abū ʿAmr, the remaining readers besides Ibn Kathīr and Nāfiʿ, and specifically ʿĀṣim, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, Ḥamza, and al-Kisāʾī. Al-Biqāʿī says the light form suggests the action was slight; Elmalılı identifies this and talahhā as shortened second-person present verbs. Al-Farrāʾ accepts a recitation of تصدى without specifying its vocalization. Ibn ʿAṭiyya names al-Aʿraj, al-Ḥasan, Abū Rajāʾ, Qatāda, ʿĪsā, and al-Aʿmash among those reading a light ṣād through deletion; Abū Ḥayyān also lists them and the majority of the seven, deriving the light form from yataṣaddā. Al-Nashr assigns the ungeminated ṣād to the remaining readers."}, {"id": "80:6/q06/p2", "position": "A doubled ṣād assimilates a tāʾ of tataṣaddā into ṣād.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj, al-Fārisī, and Ibn al-Jawzī explain assimilation, the latter citing closeness of articulation; Qirāʾāt-ER says it intensifies the onset and compresses the underlying sequence. Attributions vary: Ibn Kathīr and Nāfiʿ; the Hijaz readers; Abū Jaʿfar, Nāfiʿ, and Ibn Kathīr; Nāfiʿ and Ibn Muḥayṣin; or the two sanctuary readers. Abū Ḥayyān says the two Medinan readers and Abū ʿAmr, with qualification, double zāy and ṣād in their respective words. Al-Nashr assigns the geminated ṣād to the two Medinan readers and Ibn Kathīr; Ibn ʿAṭiyya names Ibn Kathīr and Nāfiʿ, and Abū Ḥayyān calls them the two sanctuary readers and explains assimilation of the tāʾ."}, {"id": "80:6/q06/p3", "position": "Tataṣaddā is read with both original tāʾs and a light ṣād.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī attributes this reading to Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, Abū al-Jawzāʾ, and ʿAmr ibn Dīnār. The two-tāʾ form is also the underlying form proposed by al-Zajjāj and others for the shortened and assimilated readings."}, {"id": "80:6/q06/p4", "position": "A reading begins with ḍamma on a single tāʾ and a light ṣād, allowing the sense ‘you are prompted or directed to attend to him.’", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabrisī attributes the ḍamma in this word and talahhā to Abū Jaʿfar; Ibn al-Jawzī attributes the form to Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn al-Sumayfiʿ, and al-Jaḥdarī. Al-Rāzī, al-Samīn, and al-Ālūsī attribute it to Abū Jaʿfar and explain the inner prompting as zeal for the man's conversion. Al-Samīn says the verb works both transitively and intransitively; al-Bayḍāwī allows either active turning or being summoned, while al-Ālūsī calls it passive. Al-Ṭabrisī also reports an interpretation involving worldly adornment and tidings drawing attention to the wealthy, contrasted with talahhā as turning from the blind man. Ibn Jinnī explains Abū Jaʿfar's passive form as worldly adornment drawing the Prophet toward the wealthy man. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says concern for disbelievers causes the Prophet to turn toward them; Abū Ḥayyān specifies eagerness for this man's conversion."}]}
{"id": "80:6/q07", "question": "How does this sentence sit between the two “as for” clauses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:6/q07/p1", "position": "It is parenthetical, and its wāw is parenthetical, between the self-sufficient man's clause and the eager visitor's clause.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr locates the clauses at 80:5 and 80:8."}]}
{"id": "80:6/q08", "question": "What does the conditional “as for” framing imply about this attention?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:6/q08/p1", "position": "Whenever a self-sufficient person appeared, the Prophet would turn toward him; the conditional form exaggerates the persistence of that attention.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr glosses ammā as ‘whatever may occur’ and makes its attachment to this clause a means of emphasis."}]}
{"id": "80:6/q09", "question": "What happened in the encounter behind this attention?", "turns_on": "The reports differ over the named person and, especially, who performed the censured conduct.", "positions": [{"id": "80:6/q09/p1", "position": "The Prophet attended to Quraysh leaders in hope of their conversion while Ibn Umm Maktūm repeatedly sought instruction, and turned away from him.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī says the Prophet thought the elite might reject a following made up of blind, poor, and enslaved people. Al-Biqāʿī says he hoped the wealthy man and his followers would convert and names ʿUtba, Abū Jahl, Ubayy, and Umayya ibn Khalaf among the chiefs. Ibn Kathīr says the Prophet hoped for guidance but was not accountable if the rich man failed to purify himself. Al-Durr cites another account from ʿĀʾisha: the Prophet was addressing Quraysh leaders including Abū Jahl and ʿUtba when Ibn Umm Maktūm arrived; the Prophet turned away, and the passage was revealed."}, {"id": "80:6/q09/p2", "position": "Sufyān reported that the passage was revealed concerning al-ʿAbbās.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī transmits Sufyān's report without further details in this note."}, {"id": "80:6/q09/p3", "position": "An Umayyad man with the Prophet recoiled, frowned, and turned away when Ibn Umm Maktūm came.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī quotes a report from al-Ṣādiq in al-Majmaʿ, according to which God recounted and condemned the Umayyad man's act."}]}
{"id": "80:6/q10", "question": "What guidance or rebuke does this attention convey?", "turns_on": "The notes differ on whom the rebuke ultimately targets and whether the alleged conduct can be attributed to the Prophet; they also stress different practical lessons.", "positions": [{"id": "80:6/q10/p1", "position": "The Prophet should honor and teach receptive poor seekers and warn everyone equally instead of favoring wealthy or eminent people.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUthmān, cited by al-Sulamī, says God commanded companionship with and honor for the poor and forbade love of the wealthy. Al-Qushayrī calls the passage a reproach on behalf of the poor. Ibn Kathīr includes eminent and weak, rich and poor, masters and slaves, men and women, adults and children; God guides whom He wills. Al-Iṣlāḥī says the Prophet must teach eager seekers and is not accountable for those who refuse to come. Ṭabāṭabāʾī's 80:5–12 reading contrasts scornful wealthy people unconcerned with purification and an earnest God-fearing seeker."}, {"id": "80:6/q10/p2", "position": "Pursuing a wealthy person who turns away is improper, especially given the Prophet's high station.", "reasons": "Al-Burṣawī says a noble person does not eagerly approach one who turns away. Al-Ālūsī likewise cites a verse about the impropriety of seeking the company of one who rejects yours. Al-Biqāʿī says luxury and self-sufficiency predispose rejection and wrongdoing, whereas affliction can humble and soften hearts."}, {"id": "80:6/q10/p3", "position": "The direct rebuke ultimately targets haughty leaders who ignore the message and seek exclusion of the Prophet's poor companions.", "reasons": "Al-Iṣlāḥī says those leaders wanted the poor companions removed as a condition of their own attendance, even though the Prophet is the person addressed."}, {"id": "80:6/q10/p4", "position": "Attributing disdain for the believing poor to the Prophet is untenable, whether or not a new prohibition had been revealed.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects the excuse that this became sinful only afterward: reason already condemns preferring wealth over piety, and 68:4 praises the Prophet's character. He and al-Murtaḍā invoke that character; Ṭabāṭabāʾī further cites earlier commands at 26:214–15 and 15:88, 15:94."}]}
{"id": "80:6/q11", "question": "How does this contrast fit the sūra and its neighboring sūra?", "turns_on": "The two notes identify different aspects of the sūra's connection with al-Nāziʿāt.", "positions": [{"id": "80:6/q11/p1", "position": "The sūra's call to warn those who fear is developed through resurrection, human creation, and food as signs of God's power; receptivity explains the contrast.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī relates the warning of those who fear in 79:45 to purification of receptive hearts and finds rejection astonishing in light of the signs."}, {"id": "80:6/q11/p2", "position": "ʿAbasa pairs with al-Nāziʿāt in theme, discourse style, and reasoning, while changing the order of topics.", "reasons": "Al-Iṣlāḥī cites 79:45 and says the altered sequence gives this sūra its distinct majesty."}]}
{"id": "80:6/q12", "question": "Where was Ibn Umm Maktūm at the time of the proposed encounter?", "turns_on": "Whether Ibn Umm Maktūm was already in Medina or still in Mecca when this Meccan sūra was revealed.", "positions": [{"id": "80:6/q12/p1", "position": "He was in Medina while Umayya and al-Walīd were in Mecca, so they could not have been the men involved.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī, quoted by Abū Ḥayyān, objects to the identifications on this geographic basis."}, {"id": "80:6/q12/p2", "position": "He was in Mecca before emigrating; all those figures were there when this Meccan sūra was revealed.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān rejects al-Qurṭubī's objection because Ibn Umm Maktūm was initially in Mecca and the sūra was revealed there."}]}
{"id": "80:6/q13", "question": "Who was Ibn Umm Maktūm in this account?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "80:6/q13/p1", "position": "He was ʿAbd Allāh ibn Sarḥ ibn Mālik ibn Rabīʿa al-Fihrī of Banū ʿĀmir ibn Luʾayy, Khadīja's cousin; Umm Maktūm was his paternal grandmother ʿĀtika.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān gives this name, lineage, kinship, and explanation of his designation."}]}

{"id": "80:16/q02", "question": "What does barara mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the adjective emphasizes obedience, piety, truthfulness, or benefit to others; several notes combine these senses.", "positions": [{"id": "80:16/q02/p1", "position": "Obedient to God.", "reasons": "Muqātil includes obedience, purity, righteousness, and freedom from sin. Al-Suddī, Damghānī, the exegetes reported by Ibn al-Jawzī, Baghawī, and Ibn al-Jawzī's Zād give obedience; Qushayrī combines it with righteousness. Ibn al-Jawzī illustrates the sense with 5:2, 19:14, 19:32, 58:9, and 83:18. Qurṭubī combines it with sincerity and truthfulness; Bursawī and Ālūsī offer it alongside piety and truthful oaths. Islāḥī adds faithfulness, responsibility, trustworthiness, and inability to admit devils; he mentions 26:193."}, {"id": "80:16/q02/p2", "position": "Pious, righteous, and purified.", "reasons": "Ibn Shajara says pious and purified; Ibn al-Jawzī reports a pious or righteous sense and says it could fit his category of excellence. Bayḍāwī and Nasafī say pious. Bursawī grounds piety in the angels' transcendence of matter and attachments. Muqātil adds purity and freedom from sins; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says virtuous in deed. The reciter hadith calls them pious in Study Quran. Biqāʿī describes them as pious at the highest rank of piety."}, {"id": "80:16/q02/p3", "position": "Truthful and sincere.", "reasons": "Māwardī reports al-Ṭabarī's gloss as truthful and maintaining ties or goodness. Qurṭubī derives truthfulness from birr in an oath and says the angels are sincere and truthful in deed. Bursawī and Ālūsī give truthfulness in oaths as an option."}, {"id": "80:16/q02/p4", "position": "Those whose good actions benefit others.", "reasons": "Māwardī distinguishes abrār, whose goodness extends to others, from khayyira, good only to themselves. Jishumī defines birr as beneficial good action, connecting its expansive benefit to the naming of land and wheat."}]}
{"id": "80:16/q03", "question": "What is the singular and plural formation of barara?", "turns_on": "The sources distinguish the analogical fāʿil singular from attested barr and differ over the role of abrār.", "positions": [{"id": "80:16/q03/p1", "position": "It is the plural of bārr, on the fāʿil/faʿala pattern.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ argues from kāfir/kafara and fājir/fajara, while noting actual barr usage; Ṭabarī also cites sāḥir/saḥara and heard khayr and barr. Zajjāj, Wāḥidī, Jishumī, Qurṭubī, Nasafī, and Ibn al-Jawzī report this singular or pattern. Qurṭubī lists kāfir, sāḥir, and fājir parallels. Al-Farrāʾ's sarāh example explains how actual singular usage can differ from the expected fāʿil form."}, {"id": "80:16/q03/p2", "position": "It is the plural of barr, the attested simple singular.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ heard rajul barr, imraʾa barra, and qawm khiyara barara, whose singulars are khayr and barr; he says the plural follows the sense of fāʿil. Ṭabarī likewise says Arabic normally uses barr and barra even where plural formation returns to the fāʿil pattern. Al-Rāghib and Ālūsī say barara is plural of barr; Ālūsī contrasts abrār, which can be plural of barr or bārr."}, {"id": "80:16/q03/p3", "position": "It is a collective plural of abrār, with bārr as singular.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash states this relationship."}]}
{"id": "80:16/q04", "question": "Why is barara used for angels and abrār for humans?", "turns_on": "The proposed explanations turn on plural number, comparative intensity of barr and bārr, and whether angelic or hard-won human virtue merits emphasis.", "positions": [{"id": "80:16/q04/p1", "position": "Barara is an abundance plural and abrār a paucity plural.", "reasons": "A reported view in Ālūsī and Samarrāʾī ties the forms to the greater number of pious angels. Samarrāʾī adds that all angels are righteous, whereas abrār designates righteous people."}, {"id": "80:16/q04/p2", "position": "Barara is the more emphatic form, fitting angels' superior righteousness.", "reasons": "Al-Rāghib says barr is stronger than bārr and likens barr to the intensive verbal-source adjective ʿadl; Burhān makes this depend on angelic superiority. Itqān reports the stronger bārr wording instead. Ālūsī objects that abrār can also be plural of barr and disputes that angels always warrant the stronger form."}, {"id": "80:16/q04/p3", "position": "Abrār can be more emphatic, reflecting human virtue won through struggle.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports this counterview, invoking humans' effort against innate impulses; he also disputes an unconditional claim of angelic superiority."}, {"id": "80:16/q04/p4", "position": "The Qur'anic usage reserves barara for angels and abrār for believers.", "reasons": "Samarrāʾī states the usage directly; Ālūsī says some also claim this for Qur'anic and Prophetic usage, while observing that abrār can be plural of barr or bārr."}]}
{"id": "80:16/q05", "question": "Who are the noble, righteous ones?", "turns_on": "Whether unqualified safarah in the preceding verse designates angels alone or can designate the Companions.", "positions": [{"id": "80:16/q05/p1", "position": "The angelic scribes or custodians of revelation.", "reasons": "Muqātil identifies the scribes as angels. Ibn al-ʿArabī argues that unqualified safarah designates angels specifically."}, {"id": "80:16/q05/p2", "position": "Muhammad's Companions.", "reasons": "Wahb ibn Munabbih identifies the noble righteous scribes this way. {"id": "80:16/q13", "question": "What do the poetic examples cited alongside this verse illustrate?", "turns_on": "Whether a shared poetic construction amounts to patterned borrowing, independent composition, or mere rewriting.", "positions": [{"id": "80:16/q13/p1", "position": "Poets can emulate an earlier line through shared construction even when meanings differ.", "reasons": "Jurjānī cites al-Buʿayth and al-Buḥturī as patterned borrowing. {"id": "80:17/q01", "question": "What does قُتِلَ mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether قُتِلَ retains its conventional imprecatory force, names punishment or destruction, or predicts an event; Ibn ʿAṭiyya disputes the exact gloss 'cursed'.", "positions": [{"id": "80:17/q01/p1", "position": "An imprecation against the human: may he be killed, ruined, or cursed.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Ibn Qutayba, al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatāda, Abū Mālik and others gloss it as a curse. Al-Kashshāf and Abū Ḥayyān call killing the gravest worldly calamity; Bursawī says spiritual destruction is harsher. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the expression began as a call for death, but divine imprecation conveys contempt and threat; compare passive قُتِلَ at 74:19. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ cites 74:19–20, 51:10, and 85:4. Study Quran gives 'may man perish' and reports 'may man be cursed.'"}, {"id": "80:17/q01/p2", "position": "It means the person is punished.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī transmit this alongside the curse gloss."}, {"id": "80:17/q01/p3", "position": "It means the person is destroyed.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās reasons that one who is killed has been destroyed; he also reports the curse gloss."}, {"id": "80:17/q01/p4", "position": "It describes man's self-destruction.", "reasons": "Asad points to his note on sūra 74 for this rendering."}, {"id": "80:17/q01/p5", "position": "It predicts the later killing of disbelievers, using the past tense for certainty.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports and rejects this proposal tied to the later fighting verse."}]}
{"id": "80:17/q02", "question": "What force does the curse formula have?", "turns_on": "Whether wonder belongs to the curse formula itself or only to the following exclamation; the passive follows from whether a real killer is intended.", "positions": [{"id": "80:17/q02/p1", "position": "It expresses blame, wrath, contempt, and threat, without a literal divine request.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says such formulas blame rather than ask for actual harm. Rāzī says familiar Arab speech assigns severe punishment to grave vice despite God neither lacking power nor knowledge. Ibn al-Shaykh in Bursawī likewise denies divine inability or ignorance; Ibn ʿĀshūr says people pray to God, so God's own imprecation is disparagement and threat. {"id": "80:17/q07", "question": "Why does the verse censure the human so severely?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize complementary faults: ingratitude amid divine care, proud and ungrounded denial, and inward ignorance.", "positions": [{"id": "80:17/q07/p1", "position": "He receives God's creation, guidance, care, and provisions yet responds with pride, neglect, and ingratitude.", "reasons": "Rāzī contrasts Quraysh leaders' pride with origin as a lowly drop and end as a corpse; creation proves both Creator and resurrection (80:19, 80:21), and the following account spans life's beginning, middle and end. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾ describes comprehensive governance and food as evidence of subtle mercy (14:34)."}, {"id": "80:17/q07/p2", "position": "He denies resurrection and truth without evidence, from improbability, ignorance, and stubbornness.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr calls the rejection mere improbability and ignorance. Study Quran's IK says deniers lack knowledge and find the truth far-fetched. {"id": "80:17/q08", "question": "How can divine speech express astonishment here?", "turns_on": "Whether astonishment necessarily requires an unknown cause, and whether an exclamation about divine action is assigned to God or to its human hearers.", "positions": [{"id": "80:17/q08/p1", "position": "It elicits wonder in hearers; God knows its cause, so no divine ignorance or helplessness is implied.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān prefers wonder directed at the audience and says God's knowledge of what merits wonder is called wonder; the learned explain divine exclamation, prayer and hope from the hearer's perspective, citing Sībawayh on 20:44. Abū Ḥayyān locates amazement in the human viewpoint. Bursawī says real surprise requires ignorance of a cause; Ibn al-Shaykh says the idiom conveys wrath. Al-Ālūsī calls it figurative for God. Rāzī says the familiar Arab form expresses punishment and vice."}, {"id": "80:17/q08/p2", "position": "Magnifying God in exclamatory language is permissible because it accords with belief in His greatness.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān reports the counterview and its anonymous poem that God brings what is distant near; some scholars say astonishment magnifies a matter without implying a creator of that matter, and its cause can be hidden from us."}, {"id": "80:17/q08/p3", "position": "Exclamation about God is objectionable if it suggests something made Him great, despite His eternal attributes.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān reports this view and says the dispute concerns whether true astonishment requires an unknown cause; he lists this verse with 2:175 and a reading of 82:6 among Qurʾanic exclamations."}]}

{"id": "80:18/q02", "question": "What is the force of the question about the human's origin?", "turns_on": "The notes assign several compatible rhetorical effects to the same interrogative: abasement, affirmation, challenge, reminder of favor, and anticipation; context and the answer in 80:19 are the stated cues.", "positions": [{"id": "80:18/q02/p1", "position": "It humbles the human by recalling the contemptibly low origin that makes pride and ingratitude unfitting.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī applies the challenge to a disbeliever too proud to obey or affirm oneness; Qurṭubī likewise asks how such an unbeliever can be arrogant and calls for wonder. {"id": "80:19/q02", "question": "Why describe the human origin as a drop?", "turns_on": "Whether the mention chiefly belittles the origin to rebuke pride or displays the wonder of creation as proof of resurrection; Ibn ʿĀshūr expressly denies the former emphasis.", "positions": [{"id": "80:19/q02/p1", "position": "Its lowliness rebukes human arrogance, disobedience, and ingratitude.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī calls the fluid small, base, and lifeless and asks why a person is self-deceived; he reports al-Ḥasan's reminder that a person passed twice through the urinary passage. {"id": "80:19/q05", "question": "How is 'from a drop' connected to 'He created him'?", "turns_on": "The pause after 'from a drop' and whether an implied verb is supplied before the expressed 'He created him.'", "positions": [{"id": "80:19/q05/p1", "position": "'From a drop' directly modifies 'He created him,' with no pause after the drop.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī calls this the more apparent construction and says treating 'He created him, then proportioned him' as a new sentence would duplicate the idea of measured creation."}, {"id": "80:19/q05/p2", "position": "Pause after 'from a drop,' supply an understood 'He created him,' and take 'He created him, then proportioned him' as a fresh explanation.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī reports al-Sajāwandī's pause and its supplied verb; al-Bursawī objects that this makes the ensuing new sentence redundant because creating already involves measured quantities and qualities."}]}
{"id": "80:19/q06", "question": "How does the answer relate to the preceding question?", "turns_on": "Whether the response is treated as a formal answer to a question about substance or as apposition or emphasis rather than a literal answer.", "positions": [{"id": "80:19/q06/p1", "position": "It is formally a question and answer about the substance of creation, building anticipation and directing thought to the possibility of recreation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares the anticipation to the question about the great news in 78:1–2; he says the question asks from what substance the person was made, not whether God made him, and adduces 50:15 and 86:5–8 for the analogy to resurrection."}, {"id": "80:19/q06/p2", "position": "The answer is not a literal answer but an apposition to the question, or an emphatic restatement.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī offers apposition and, alternatively, emphasis; he says the indefinite 'thing' or 'drop' supplies the belittling force."}]}

{"id": "80:19/q08", "question": "What does 'then proportioned him' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the measure concerns fitting bodily and mental design, prenatal developmental stages, allotted life and destiny, or stages across the lifespan; several sources combine these senses.", "positions": [{"id": "80:19/q08/p1", "position": "God fashioned and fitted the human's body, organs, qualities, and capacities in precise proportions.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and those reporting him describe a proper or upright form and cite 18:37; al-Qurṭubī also cites 82:7. Al-Wāḥidī's Wajīz continues to birth and mentions 80:20; al-Bayḍāwī, al-Bursawī, and al-Ālūsī present this as an alternative to fitting form and organs."}, {"id": "80:19/q08/p3", "position": "God apportioned each person's sex, lifespan, provision, deeds, and fortune or misery.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ combines male or female and wretched or blessed with fetal stages; Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds organs, lifespan, and other matters according to divine will. Al-Bursawī links sex and fortune to development, and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī extends divine measure to human acts and allotted limits."}, {"id": "80:19/q08/p4", "position": "God measured the gradual stages of human life from childhood through youth to old age.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī compares these life stages to the moon's phases in 36:39 and adduces 23:12–16; their order points to divine power, purpose, resurrection, and judgment."}]}
